title: A presence
hookLine: Wordsworth felt a presence that disturbed him with joy
carry: a joy strong enough to unsettle
tomorrow: A world in a grain of sand

cards: "Five years have past; five summers, with the length of five long winters!" That's how the poem opens.

William Wordsworth is back on the banks of the river Wye, a few miles above Tintern Abbey, looking at a landscape he last saw five years before. Same cliffs, same quiet, same smoke rising from the trees.
But he isn't the same, and the poem is about the difference. When he tries to say what this place has given him, what comes out isn't a view at all. It's a presence.

teach.b: Here are his words: "And I have felt a presence that disturbs me with the joy of elevated thoughts; a sense sublime of something far more deeply interfused, whose dwelling is the light of setting suns, and the round ocean and the living air, and the blue sky, and in the mind of man".
First, the odd verb. The presence disturbs him, and what it disturbs him with is joy. Not calm, not comfort: a joy strong enough to unsettle.
Kant spoke of admiration and awe; Wordsworth adds that awe can shake a person, even when it's glad.
Second, interfused. The presence isn't standing outside the world, looking in. It's mixed through things, the way light is mixed through air.
Third, the address list: setting suns, the round ocean, the living air, the blue sky. Ordinary things anyone can see on a clear evening.
Fourth, the last stop: the mind of man.
The same presence that lives in the sunset lives in the one watching it. And notice what Wordsworth never does in these lines. He doesn't give it a name.
He says presence. He says something. Some readers hear God in it; some hear nature; some hear both.
The poem leaves it unnamed, and seems to want it that way.

how: Some people on a personal spiritual path keep a habit of slow walks outdoors, and readers of Wordsworth often return to this passage from Tintern Abbey as a way of naming moments of awe in nature.

o: something unnamed Wordsworth felt mixed through sky, sea and mind
the memory of his younger self, standing in the same valley
a ghost Wordsworth believed haunted the ruins of Tintern Abbey

p: with the joy of elevated thoughts

s: Wordsworth says the presence brings him only calm
he says it "disturbs me with the joy of elevated thoughts."
the passage places the presence in the mind as well as the sky
its dwelling ends: "and in the mind of man."
in these lines Wordsworth names the presence as God
he calls it a presence and "something far more deeply interfused", and leaves it unnamed.

games.q: you're Wordsworth, back above the river after five years away. you try to say what this place has given you. what comes out?
o: a list of what has changed in the view.
a presence that disturbs you with joy.
a wish never to come back.
games.why: he writes of "a presence that disturbs me with the joy of elevated thoughts", living in sunsets, ocean, air, sky and the mind.

practice: Walk slowly outdoors at half your normal speed, or slowly across a room, or stand at an open window. Don't look for anything in particular; let the light, the air and the sky do what they do.
If a moment stirs you a little, let it, and if nothing comes, that's part of it too.

wordCard.voice: A presence. Wordsworth's name for something he couldn't name, living in sunsets, ocean, air and sky, and in the mind that sees them. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: a joy strong enough to unsettle. Wordsworth never named it, and he didn't need to. See you tomorrow.
